$comment: Ground truth for fixture `vendor-listener`: what a correct attribution must
say about the frame this app produces. The accuracy suite reads this file; it
is the fixture's contract, not documentation of it.
This fixture is unusual in that the contract has two halves that disagree.
`expected.slices[].loafAttributesTo` is what LoAF will say, and
`expected.slices[].trueOwner` is what is true. For two of the three slices
those are the same file; for the vendor slice they are not, and that gap is
the finding. Collapsing them into one answer would make the fixture
unfalsifiable: a tool that reported the frame as 100% first-party would pass.
`expectedSourceText` exists so the ground truth validates itself. Line numbers
drift the moment someone edits a file, and a stale line number fails as a
wrong attribution rather than as a broken fixture. A test asserts that each
recorded line still contains the recorded text before it asserts anything
about the tool's output. The three registration lines are byte-identical, so
each slice records the line below it as well — that one is unique.
title: Three sibling listeners, one of them a third party's

bug.summary: One button carries three separate click listeners. A single click runs first-party compute, a pretend third-party analytics call, and a forced-layout thrash over 400 rows, all inside one event dispatch and therefore inside one animation frame.
bug.whyItIsRealistic: Listeners accumulate. Feature code adds one, an analytics wrapper adds another, and a layout-dependent widget adds a third; nobody writes the slow frame, it assembles itself. The vendor call in particular is the ordinary shape of an analytics tag: first-party code registers the listener and calls into the vendor's global.
whatItIsFor: Claim 1: `sourceCharPosition` is valuable outside a framework. All three LoAF entries have an empty `sourceFunctionName` (anonymous arrows), so the character offset is the only attribution available — and it lands in the user's own file, not in a dispatcher. Contrast `derive-in-render`, where LoAF names only react-dom's `dispatchDiscreteEvent`.

Claim 2: LoAF's script attribution cannot produce a third-party share. The vendor slice is attributed to `app.js`, because that is where its listener was registered; `vendor.js` appears in no field of the LoAF entry. Wherever first-party code calls into a vendor library, LoAF's share is first-party by construction, so a third-party share requires the profiler.
bug.promotedFrom: spike/archive/vanilla, the throwaway fixture behind findings.md, "What made it hard", point 5. The predecessor also carried a second button that rebuilt 4,000 rows via innerHTML, for the unrelated browser-work-residual finding; that half was dropped on promotion so this fixture janks for exactly one reason.

interaction.description: Click the button once. One click, three listeners, one frame.
$comment: `data-fixture` is the only selector contract; the predecessor's `id="go"` was
dropped, which is why `observedJank` cannot carry its `invoker` string over.
LoAF composes `invoker` from the element's tag, id and classes, so removing
the id changes a reported field.

reproduction.note: Every millisecond figure derived from this fixture must be quoted with these two settings. Two of the three slices are wall-clock budgeted and so barely move with the throttle rate, while the forced layout is real browser work and scales with it — so the throttle rate does not just scale this fixture's numbers, it changes the frame's composition.

$comment: The predecessor janked only on the first click of a page load, and did so
silently. It wrote a padding value derived from the row index alone, so from
the second click onwards the same value was written to the same rows, style
was never invalidated, and `offsetHeight` cost nothing: in `vanilla4.json`,
six clicks produced a single long frame. This fixture mixes a run counter
into the padding so every click genuinely forces layout, which is what makes
a replay possible — and findings.md is clear that replay is what turns
single-frame line attribution into a stable distribution.
Three listeners, three script entries, in registration order. Three siblings
are the cheapest way to get a frame with more than one slice at all: nested
entry points are merged by spec — a new script entry is not started while one
is pending — which is why React's whole render arrives as one entry in
`derive-in-render`. One listener calling three functions would do the same.
Entries under 5ms are not reported, so all three slices are deliberately well
clear of that floor.

loafAttributesTo.nextLineExpectedSourceText: // slice 1 of 3: first-party compute, truly owned by computeTotals below
$comment: `sourceCharPosition` is measured, against this fixture's own served text,
and verified by the accuracy suite: resolving it with `lineColumnAt` over
the repo's copy of app.js lands on the line recorded above. That check is
possible at all because app.js is served from public/, which Vite copies
byte-for-byte, so the repo's copy IS the served text - identically in both
build modes. The predecessor's offsets (1336, 1422, 1509) were measured
against a different, shorter app.js and were deliberately not carried over.
`sourceFunctionName` is the empty string by construction, not by
measurement: the callback is an anonymous arrow. It is part of the
contract because it is what forces the character offset to do the work.

trueOwner.note: LoAF names the registration line; the cost is one line of indirection away, in a first-party function in the same file. This is the easy case, and it is here as the control for the vendor slice.

loafAttributesTo.nextLineExpectedSourceText: // slice 2 of 3: truly owned by vendor.js, which LoAF will not mention
$comment: Measured, as above. This is the entry the fixture exists for: every field
LoAF populates here points at `app.js`, and no field mentions `vendor.js`
at all. The attribution is not imprecise, it is about the wrong file, and
resolving the offset more carefully cannot fix it — the registration site
really is in `app.js`. A third-party share needs the profiler.

trueOwner.note: A separately-fetched classic script with its own sourceURL, untransformed by Vite because it is served from public/. Reached as a global from the first-party listener, which is how analytics tags are actually wired up.

$declaredTierComment: tier above, in the engine's AttributionTier vocabulary. `Unmapped` adds
no claim: trueOwner.note says vendor.js is served from public/,
untransformed, and `why` says the samples name vendor.js and vendorTrack
directly - as served, with no source map to resolve through, which is
what the engine calls profiler-unmapped. Both modes, because Vite copies
public/ byte-for-byte in a production build too (observedJank.$measured).
recoverableFrom.why: Sampled stacks carry a resource id per frame, so samples inside the vendor's hot loop name `vendor.js` and `vendorTrack` directly. LoAF cannot: it reports one registration site per listener and has no field for what that listener went on to call.
$comment: Note the sampling floor when asserting on this: 5ms requested becomes 10ms,
which measured out at a 12.2ms median cadence in one corpus capture and
14.5ms in the next (findings.md, point 1; 4x), so a 12ms vendor
slice is about one sample. The share is only stable over a replay, and a
per-frame percentage for this slice is not a fair assertion.

loafAttributesTo.nextLineExpectedSourceText: // slice 3 of 3: forced layout, the dominant cost of the frame
$comment: Measured, as above.

forcingLines.role: invalidates style and layout for this row

forcingLines.expectedSourceText: total += row.offsetHeight; // forces style and layout, every iteration
forcingLines.role: demands a clean layout tree immediately after invalidating it; this is the line the cost belongs to

trueOwner.note: Most of this slice's duration is not JavaScript at all but browser layout work the script provoked. Sampled stacks inside it are expected to be sparse or empty, which is the cross-check rather than a failure: an empty stack means no JS was running, not that nothing happened.

$comment: The trap this fixture pins down, from findings.md, "Decomposing the frame":
`forcedStyleAndLayoutDuration` on the third entry is browser work nested
INSIDE that entry's own `duration`, not a sibling of it. Adding it as a
fourth slice double-counts the largest cost in the frame — on the
predecessor that was ~107ms of a ~150ms frame, so the arithmetic would
report well over 100% of the frame as accounted for.
The rendering-phase fields stay at zero for the same reason: style and
layout performed inside a script are reported as the script's forced figure,
while `styleDuration` and `layoutDuration` count only the frame's own
rendering update. Both were 0 in all four predecessor runs. That is
specified behaviour, not a Chrome bug.
frameDecomposition.honestSum: startTime→scripts[0].startTime (pre-script) + Σ scripts[i].duration + (renderStart − last script end) + style/layout/paint of the rendering update, with forcedStyleAndLayoutDuration NEVER added.

mustName: three distinct slices of the one frame, ranked with the forced layout first
`app.js` as the registration site of all three, at lines 188, 192 and 196
`vendor.js` as the true owner of the second slice, at whatever confidence the available tier supports
mustNotName: a single culprit for the frame
`vendor.js` for the first or third slice
a share of the frame that attributes the vendor slice's cost to first-party code
acceptableAttribution.note: The degenerate single-culprit shape is wrong here even if it picks the forced layout: the forced layout is the largest slice, not the whole frame. This fixture is the concrete case for the `frame → ranked candidate causes with weights` invariant.

notAtFault.note: Nothing in this fixture is innocent-but-accused in the way `derive-in-render`'s App is; the failure modes here are about the shape of the answer rather than the identity of a bystander.

failureModesThisFixtureTestsFor.why: Every LoAF field for the vendor slice says `app.js`, so a tool that trusts LoAF's script attribution for provenance reports the third party as having done nothing at all. This is the specific failure the fixture exists to catch.

The same error stated as a share. Roughly 8% of the predecessor's frame was a third party's code, and LoAF alone will put that 8% in the first-party column rather than in an unattributed one. Reporting it as first-party is worse than reporting it as unknown.
See `expected.frameDecomposition`. It makes the slices sum past the frame duration, which also destroys any honest `unattributed` remainder.

failureModesThisFixtureTestsFor.failure: collapsing the three entries into one cause
failureModesThisFixtureTestsFor.why: All three share an invoker and a source file, so a naive grouping key merges them into one 140ms `app.js` cause and loses both of this fixture's findings at once.

Measured from the captures currently in corpus/vendor-listener. Chromium
159.0.8154.6 on Apple silicon, 4x CPU throttling, six clicks per mode.
Ranges rather than per-frame arrays; per-frame values are in the corpus.
Development and production agree to noise, and that is structural rather
than lucky: both scripts are served from public/, which Vite copies
byte-for-byte, so the character offsets index the same text in both modes.
That is also what lets the accuracy suite resolve those offsets against
the repo's own copy of app.js with no capture of the text at all.
sourceCharPositions resolve to the three registration lines declared under
expected.slices. sourceFunctionNames are empty on all three because the
listeners are anonymous arrows, which is what forces the character offset
to do the work. sourceURLs contains only app.js: the vendor owns one of
these three slices entirely and LoAF never names vendor.js, because it
attributes to the registration site. A third-party share is not available
from this signal - it needs the profiler.
forcedStyleAndLayoutDuration is nested INSIDE the third slice's duration.
Adding it as a separate slice double-counts.
`invokerType` is spec-determined and safe to declare. `invoker` is null
because the predecessor's "BUTTON#go.onclick" cannot be carried over: this
fixture's button has no id, and LoAF builds the string from the element's
tag, id and classes. `sourceFunctionName` is expected to be the empty string
on all three entries, declared under `expected` as a contract; it is null
here because this section is reserved for what was measured.
All three entries are expected to share one invoker, which is what makes the
fourth failure mode above easy to walk into.
